title: Exact treewidth

problem.name: Treewidth
problem.statement_latex:
For a graph $G$, find a tree decomposition $(T,\{B_t\})$ minimizing $\max_t|B_t|-1$. Every vertex belongs to a bag, every edge has both endpoints in a bag, and the bags containing each vertex induce a connected subtree. Treewidth governs the complexity of many graph and constraint algorithms.
The polynomial-space quantum bound counts gate time, the exponential-memory quantum bounds use QRAM time, and classical bounds use RAM time.
problem.statement_text: For a graph $G$, find a tree decomposition $(T,\{B_t\})$ minimizing $\max_t|B_t|-1$. Every vertex belongs to a bag, every edge has both endpoints in a bag, and the bags containing each vertex induce a connected subtree. Treewidth governs the complexity of many graph and constraint algorithms. The polynomial-space quantum bound counts gate time, the exponential-memory quantum bounds use QRAM time, and classical bounds use RAM time.

quantum.headline_latex: $O^*(1.538^n)$ with exponential QRAM, quantum treewidth dynamic programming.
quantum.details_latex: K\c{l}evickis--Pr\=usis--Vihrovs also give $O^*(1.554^n)$ time with $O^*(1.452^n)$ space, and $O^*(1.618^n)$ time with polynomial space. The fastest variant uses $O^*(1.538^n)$ space. These are distinct memory tradeoffs obtained from separator-based structural decompositions and quantum search.
quantum.headline_text: $O^*(1.538^n)$ with exponential QRAM, quantum treewidth dynamic programming.
quantum.details_text: Kļevickis–Prūsis–Vihrovs also give $O^*(1.554^n)$ time with $O^*(1.452^n)$ space, and $O^*(1.618^n)$ time with polynomial space. The fastest variant uses $O^*(1.538^n)$ space. These are distinct memory tradeoffs obtained from separator-based structural decompositions and quantum search.

classical.headline_latex: $O^*(1.7347^n)$ with exponential space, potential-maximal-clique dynamic programming; $O^*(2.6151^n)$ with polynomial space, Fomin--Villanger.
classical.details_latex: The first bound enumerates potential maximal cliques and optimizes compatible decomposition blocks. The polynomial-space method enumerates connected sets with constrained neighborhoods and recursively assembles decompositions. The comparison with the polynomial-space quantum algorithm therefore uses the $2.6151^n$ bound; the $1.538^n$ quantum algorithm uses the exponential-space comparison.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedups through smaller exponential constants in both displayed memory regimes. The quantum constructions combine structural enumeration with amplitude amplification and minimum finding.
strength.description_text: Polynomial speedups through smaller exponential constants in both displayed memory regimes. The quantum constructions combine structural enumeration with amplitude amplification and minimum finding.

evidence.description_latex: Rigorous time-space bounds and partial evidence relative to the best classical algorithms for the same space regime.
evidence.description_text: Rigorous time-space bounds and partial evidence relative to the best classical algorithms for the same space regime.

hardware.description_latex: The fastest quantum construction needs exponential coherent memory and polynomial active graph registers. The $1.618^n$ variant reduces storage to polynomial logical workspace but retains exponential coherent running time. Fault tolerance is needed in either useful regime.

Theorems 21, 22 and 24 give the three tradeoffs; Algorithm 4 gives the fastest construction. Algorithm 1 states the classical polynomial-space procedure.
